pos: n. (the Emilian city of Europe's oldest university, of the 1530 imperial coronation of Charles the Fifth, and of the council of Trent's brief transfer in 1547)
etymology: From Latin Bononia, a Roman colony on an earlier Etruscan and Boian site.
biblical_def: Bologna held the oldest university in Europe, a school of law from the late eleventh century whose glossators recovered the Roman civil law and whose canonists, Gratian above all, assembled the body of church law that governed the medieval West. Gratian's Decretum, compiled at Bologna about 1140, is the book that made canon law a science, and with it came the machinery of dispensations, reserved cases and papal jurisdiction that the Reformers would spend their lives arguing against. In 1530 Charles the Fifth was crowned emperor in the church of San Petronio by Clement the Seventh, the last imperial coronation performed by a pope. In 1547 the council of Trent was transferred to Bologna on the plea of plague; the imperial bishops refused to follow, and the council was suspended. The dictionary records Bologna as the place where the church learned to think like a court. Law in the church is not the enemy; the New Testament has order, offices and discipline. What Bologna supplied was a jurisprudence in which the pope held the interpretive key, so that a question of conscience became a question of jurisdiction, and the text stopped being the final appeal.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canon as a law or rule of the church; a decree as an ordinance made by superior authority; jurisdiction as the legal power of governing; a dispensation as a relaxation of law; and conscience as the internal judge of right and wrong.
webster_full: CANON, n. In church affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.
DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior as a rule to govern inferiors.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty, power or principle within us, which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
corruption_summary: Emilian city of Europe's oldest university, where Gratian's canon-law compilation gave the medieval church a jurisprudence with the pope as interpretive key.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the replacement of a rule of faith by a system of jurisdiction. Once the decisive question is who has authority to decide, rather than what is written, the text can be honoured in theory and bypassed in practice, which is how dispensations and reserved cases came to govern Christian consciences. Christ names the mechanism when he quotes Isaiah against the scribes of his own day: “But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The dictionary does not blame the recovery of Roman law for the abuse; it blames the decision to make a court the last word.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is a fixed deposit and a final appeal. Moses forbids both addition and subtraction in the plainest terms, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32), and Isaiah supplies the test that any canon must pass: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The woe Christ pronounces on the lawyers of Israel is the exact woe the Reformers pronounced on the canonists, that a learned class had made itself a gate: “for ye have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luk 11:52). Law in the church must serve the text, or it will quietly replace it.

Greek mataios (G3152) — empty, vain, to no purpose; “But in vain they do worship me”, Matthew 15:9.

“thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32) — the fixed deposit canon law must serve.
“ye have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luk 11:52) — the Reformers' charge against the canonists.

pos: n. (the Emilian city and Farnese duchy created in 1545 for the son of Paul the Third, the plainest monument of papal nepotism)
etymology: From Latin Parma, a Roman colony, the name perhaps from a small round shield of that name.
biblical_def: Parma is a city of the Emilian plain which in 1545 became, with Piacenza, a hereditary duchy carved out of the papal state by Paul the Third and granted to his son Pier Luigi Farnese. The grant was made in the same decade in which that pope reorganised the Roman Inquisition and summoned the council of Trent to reform the church; it was opposed in consistory, and Pier Luigi was murdered by his nobles two years later. The Farnese dukes held Parma until 1731. The dictionary records Parma as the clearest single instance of papal nepotism, because here the office did not merely enrich a relative but manufactured a sovereign state for an illegitimate son out of lands held in trust for the church. The Reformation's objection to the Roman system was never only doctrinal. It was that an office with no accountability and vast revenues will be used for a family, and that this is not an accident of bad popes but the predictable working of unchecked power. Trent legislated against some abuses; it left the institution that produced Parma untouched.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nepotism as fondness for nephews or relations; a duchy as the territory of a duke; a trust as something committed to one's care; revenue as the annual income of a state; and simony as the buying or selling of church preferment.
webster_full: NEPOTISM, n. Fondness for nephews; undue attachment and partiality to relations, especially in the bestowment of offices.
DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
TRUST, n. Something committed to a person's care for use or management, and for which an account must be rendered.
REVENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property; the annual income of a state.
SIMONY, n. The crime of buying or selling ecclesiastical preferment, or of corruptly presenting to a benefice.
scriptures: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Emilian city made a hereditary Farnese duchy in 1545 for the son of Paul the Third, carved out of lands held in trust for the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is nepotism, and the dictionary names it as theft of a trust rather than as mere favouritism. The lands that became Parma were not Paul the Third's to give; they were held for the church, and they were converted into a family inheritance by a man whose office was pastoral. Peter's charge to elders forbids exactly the motive and the manner: feed the flock “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2), and Paul reminds overseers whose property the church is, “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that church office is stewardship under audit. The qualifications Paul lists for a bishop include being “not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:3), and the reason is not that money is unclean but that a man who wants it will sell the flock to get it. The prophet reduces the whole requirement of an officeholder to three things that leave no room for a duchy: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The dictionary observes that Trent reformed residence, preaching and seminaries, and did not touch the arrangement by which a pope could father a duke.

“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — whose property a pope was giving away.
“to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8) — the whole requirement of office.

pos: n. (the Emilian city joined with Parma in the 1545 Farnese duchy, and seat of the 1095 council at which Urban the Second first raised the crusade)
etymology: From Latin Placentia, the pleasing place, from placere, to please.
biblical_def: Piacenza guards the crossing of the Po on the road from Milan to Bologna, and it has two entries in church history. In March 1095 Urban the Second held a council there which heard the Byzantine emperor's appeal for help against the Turks; the response was taken up and enlarged at Clermont in November of the same year, and the first crusade followed. In 1545 the city was joined with Parma into the hereditary duchy granted to Pier Luigi Farnese, and the citizens of Piacenza were among those most hostile to the new duke, who was killed at Piacenza in 1547. The dictionary treats the first of these as the weightier matter. The crusade introduced into Western Christianity the idea of an armed pilgrimage whose participants were promised remission of sin, and that promise is the seed of the indulgence traffic that Luther attacked four centuries later. The dictionary does not dispute that nations may wage just wars; it denies that any war can be a sacrament, or that dying under arms can purchase what Christ purchased.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crusade as a military expedition against infidels; remission as the forgiveness of sin; a pilgrimage as a journey to a holy place; an indulgence as a remission of penalty; and atonement as the expiation of sin by the satisfaction offered.
webster_full: CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by christians for the recovery of the Holy Land from the infidels.
REMISSION, n. Forgiveness; pardon; that is, the giving up of the punishment due to a crime.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.
INDULGENCE, n. In the Romish church, remission of the punishment due to sins, granted by the pope or church.
ATONEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
scriptures: For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: Emilian city of the 1095 council at which Urban the Second first raised the crusade, and half of the 1545 Farnese duchy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the crusade indulgence, and through it the whole notion that a man may add something to the satisfaction of Christ. Piacenza heard the first appeal; Clermont turned it into a promise of remitted penance for those who took the cross, and that promise was later extended, sold and finally printed. The doctrine that answers it is the finality of one sacrifice: “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). An offering that has perfected for ever cannot be supplemented by a march, a payment or a death in battle.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Hebrews marks the completion of the work by the posture of the priest, who sits because there is nothing left to offer: “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12). There is accordingly one mediator and no second channel, “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). As to the method, the dictionary holds that the church's warfare is real and its weapons are not steel, since “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). A state may justly defend itself; a church may never bless an army as a means of grace.

“sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12) — the posture that ends the offering.
“one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5) — no second channel of merit.

pos: n. (the Lombard city on the Po, a Guelf commune of the Lombard League and the home of the Amati and Stradivari violin makers)
etymology: From Latin Cremona, a Roman colony of 218 before Christ, the name of Celtic or Etruscan origin.
biblical_def: Cremona stands on the north bank of the Po in Lombardy, a Roman colony, a free commune, and a member of the Lombard League that resisted Frederick Barbarossa in the twelfth century, though it changed sides more than once. Its lasting fame is in instruments: the Amati family from the fifteen-hundreds, then Guarneri and Antonio Stradivari, whose workshops made the violins that still set the standard of the craft. The city came under Milan in the fourteenth century and followed Milan's fortunes through the Spanish and Austrian periods. The dictionary records Cremona for the sake of an argument it wants to make plainly. Reformed worship restrained instruments in the sanctuary, and in some places excluded them altogether, and that restraint was a judgment about the regulation of public worship, not a verdict on music. A Cremonese violin is a lawful and admirable thing, made by patient men out of wood and varnish for the delight of their neighbours. The question the Reformers asked was narrower and sharper: what has God appointed for the assembly of his people?
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an instrument as a tool or implement, and in music a machine for producing sound; a craft as a manual art; melody as an agreeable succession of sounds; worship as the act of paying divine honours; and appointment as the act of fixing by authority.
webster_full: INSTRUMENT, n. A tool; that by which work is performed; in music, an artificial machine or body by which sounds are produced.
CRAFT, n. Art; ability; dexterity; manual art; trade; the occupation of an artificer.
MELODY, n. An agreeable succession of sounds; a succession of sounds so regulated as to please the ear.
WORSHIP, n. The act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; religious reverence and homage.
APPOINTMENT, n. The act of appointing; designation to office; stipulation; direction; established order or constitution.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: Lombard city on the Po, home of the Amati, Guarneri and Stradivari workshops, and the dictionary's occasion for stating the rule of worship plainly.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover concerns the regulation of public worship, and it must be stated without the sourness that often attends it. Scripture governs the assembly by appointment rather than by taste, and Paul states the governing instinct for the whole chapter on public order in one line: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Moses forbids both adding and taking away, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32), and the reason the Reformed churches were severe here is that worship is the one activity where human invention has done the most damage.

The second paragraph names the live temptation on both sides. One error treats the sanctuary as a concert hall where excellence is its own warrant; the other treats a craftsman's skill as worldliness, which Scripture nowhere teaches. Christ gives the standard in terms that answer both: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24). What is condemned is not beauty but invention substituted for command, “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). A Cremonese violin is a good gift of God; whether it belongs in the Lord's day assembly is a question of appointment, and the dictionary insists on keeping the two questions apart.

“they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24) — the standard that answers both errors.
“thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32) — why invention is the danger, not beauty.

pos: n. (the Lombard city under Venetian rule whose evangelical circle of the fifteen-forties was broken by the Inquisition, and home of the Somascan and Ursuline foundations)
etymology: From Latin Brixia, a Cenomani town, the name from a Celtic root for a height.
biblical_def: Brescia lies at the foot of the Alps between Milan and Verona, and from 1426 to 1797 it was a Venetian city, which mattered because Venetian law resisted Roman jurisdiction and left a little more room than Lombardy under Spain. In the fifteen-forties Brescia had an evangelical circle, and the Inquisition worked there through the following decade. The city also produced two sixteenth-century Roman foundations of real seriousness: the Somascan clerks under Jerome Emiliani, who gathered orphans, and the Company of Saint Ursula under Angela Merici in 1535, which organised unmarried women to teach girls. The dictionary records both sides without blending them. Brescia shows that the Roman church of the Catholic Reformation was not merely reactionary; it answered real needs that the medieval parish had neglected, above all the teaching of children. It also shows that this energy was deliberately channelled away from the question the evangelicals had raised, which was how a sinner is accepted. Charity without that answer is a kindness that leaves a man where he was.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines charity as liberality to the poor; an orphan as a child bereaved of parents; a catechism as a form of instruction by questions; instruction as the act of teaching; and acceptance as the receiving with approbation.
webster_full: CHARITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; liberality to the poor, consisting in almsgiving or benefactions.
ORPHAN, n. A child who is bereaved of father or mother or of both.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
INSTRUCTION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; information; direction.
ACCEPTANCE, n. A receiving with approbation or satisfaction; favorable reception.
scriptures: Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Venetian-ruled Lombard city of an evangelical circle broken by the Inquisition, and of the Somascan and Ursuline foundations for orphans and the teaching of girls.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the substitution of charity for the gospel, which is the most respectable error available to a church. Brescia's sixteenth-century foundations fed orphans and taught girls, and the dictionary honours both, since James makes visiting the fatherless a mark of real religion: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27). But the question raised in that same decade by the Brescian evangelicals was not whether the church should be kind. It was how a man stands before God, and Paul's answer is a conclusion, not an opinion: “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Works of mercy are the fruit of justification and cannot be its root, and Paul states the exclusion twice over so that no reader can miss it: “for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified” (Gal 2:16). The other thing the Ursulines got right and the dictionary wants kept is the duty of plain teaching, which Nehemiah's Levites model exactly: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). Teach the children, feed the orphans, and tell them how a sinner is accepted.

“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — what the Brescian foundations got right.
“and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — the model for teaching children.

pos: n. (the Lombard city under Venice whose upper town kept a Guelf and the lower a Venetian character, and a station on the smuggling road by which Reformation books entered Italy)
etymology: From Latin Bergomum, from a Celtic or Ligurian root meaning a height or fortress.
biblical_def: Bergamo sits on the first rise of the Alpine foothills north-east of Milan and was Venetian from 1428 until 1797, a border city looking across at Spanish Lombardy. Border cities matter in the history of the Reformation because books cross borders. The route from the German and Swiss presses into Italy ran through the Alpine valleys above Bergamo, Brescia and Como, by way of the Valtellina and the Grisons, and the merchants and muleteers of these towns carried Luther, Bucer, Calvin and, above all, cheap Italian translations of evangelical tracts southward in bales. The Venetian government winked at a good deal of this while it suited Venice to be independent of Rome. The dictionary records Bergamo for the sake of a principle the Reformation had to learn under pressure: that the word of God travels by ordinary means, in the packs of men who are not clergy, and that no frontier has ever successfully closed against a book. The Inquisition's index of prohibited books is the clearest confession that this is true.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a book as a printed volume; a press as the machine for printing; a frontier as the border of a country; smuggling as importing goods secretly; and an index as a table of contents or list.
webster_full: BOOK, n. A general name of every literary composition which is printed; but appropriately, a printed composition bound in a volume.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed, crushed or forced into a more compact form; a printing press.
FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
SMUGGLE, v.t. To import or export secretly goods which are forbidden by the government to be imported or exported.
INDEX, n. A table of the contents of a book; in the Romish church, a list of prohibited books.
scriptures: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
But the word of God grew and multiplied.
corruption_summary: Venetian border city in the Lombard foothills, a station on the Alpine smuggling route by which Reformation books entered Italy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freedom of the word under censorship, and the Alpine book trade is its best historical illustration. Rome issued an index of prohibited books, posted guards on passes, searched bales at Venice and burned what it found, and Italian evangelicals went on reading. Paul had made the point from a cell in a sentence that fits the whole episode: “Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9).

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to think the word's advance requires extraordinary means. It does not. Luke credits scattered laymen with the first great expansion, “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and he sums up a whole chapter of persecution with a line about the text rather than the persecutors: “But the word of God grew and multiplied” (Act 12:24). The promise attached to the word binds God to his own sending, not to our conditions, since it “shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). Muleteers with bales are an ordinary means, and they were enough.

Greek auxano (G0837) — to grow, to increase; “But the word of God grew and multiplied”, Acts 12:24.
Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad; “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word”, Acts 8:4.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a thing spoken; “So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth”, Isaiah 55:11.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper, to succeed; “it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it”, Isaiah 55:11.

“But the word of God grew and multiplied” (Act 12:24) — Luke's summary of a persecution.
“it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” (Isa 55:11) — why ordinary means suffice.

pos: n. (the Lombard city of the Gonzaga, named in 1537 as the first site of the general council later held at Trent, and the diocese of Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga)
etymology: From Latin Mantua, an Etruscan town name, traditionally derived from the god Mantus.
biblical_def: Mantua lies on the Mincio in a loop of lakes, and was governed by the Gonzaga family from 1328 until 1708. In 1537 Paul the Third summoned a general council to meet at Mantua, and that summons is the reason the city belongs in this dictionary: the Protestant princes refused the venue as being in imperial Italy and under papal control, Duke Federico demanded a garrison at papal expense, and the council was postponed, moved to Vicenza, postponed again, and finally opened at Trent in 1545. The eight years of manoeuvre between Mantua and Trent were decisive, because by 1545 the Protestant churches were organised, confessed and governed, and no longer needed the council they had demanded in 1520. The diocese of Mantua was held from 1521 by Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga, a reform-minded prelate who presided at Trent in its final period and died there in 1563. The dictionary records Mantua as the price of delay: a reform postponed for the convenience of princes became a reform refused.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an ecclesiastical assembly; a summons as a call by authority to appear; delay as a putting off or deferring; a venue as the place where a cause is tried; and reform as a change from worse to better.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice, especially an assembly of ecclesiastics.
SUMMONS, n. A call by authority or the command of a superior to appear at a place named, or to attend to some duty.
DELAY, n. A putting off or deferring; procrastination; a lingering; stay; stop.
VENUE, n. In law, a neighborhood or near place; the place where an action is laid or a cause tried.
REFORM, n. A change from worse to better; amendment of life or manners; correction of abuses.
scriptures: Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Pro 27:1
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
Heb 3:15
While it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.
corruption_summary: Gonzaga city named in 1537 as the first site of the general council, whose postponement for eight years ended at Trent in 1545.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of procedure to avoid a question, and Mantua is the textbook case. Christendom had asked for a free general council since 1520; a pope summoned one in 1537 to a city of imperial Italy, a duke demanded terms, the Protestants objected to the venue, and eight years went by in negotiation while positions hardened on both sides. Nobody in that process said no to reform. Everyone said not here and not yet. Felix's famous adjournment is the same move in one sentence: “Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee” (Act 24:25).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that repentance has a clock. The Lord's word to a declining church is not a proposal to be scheduled but a command with a term attached, “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5), and the writer to the Hebrews fixes the day: “To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts” (Heb 3:15). Solomon forbids the confidence that makes delay feel safe, “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Pro 27:1). A church may be lost by a calendar as surely as by a heresy.

pos: n. (the Este duchy whose duchess Renee sheltered evangelicals and corresponded with Calvin, and seat of the council of 1438 before its transfer to Florence)
etymology: From medieval Latin Ferraria, a place of iron workings, from ferrum, iron.
biblical_def: Ferrara was the capital of the Este dukes on the lower Po, a court of considerable learning, and from 1528 the home of Renee of France, daughter of Louis the Twelfth, who married Ercole the Second of Este. Renee held evangelical convictions, kept Protestant servants and tutors, corresponded with Calvin for thirty years, and sheltered men passing through Italy, among them Calvin himself in 1536 under an assumed name and Clement Marot the psalm-versifier. Her husband, pressed by Rome and by his need of French and papal favour, had her examined in 1554; she conformed under duress and was for a time separated from her children. On Ercole's death she returned to France, settled at Montargis, and sheltered Huguenots there through the wars until her death in 1575. The council transferred from Basel met at Ferrara in 1438 before moving to Florence. The dictionary records Ferrara chiefly for Renee, a princess who did what very few of her rank did: she used a court as a refuge, held her convictions through a forced recantation, and resumed them the moment she could.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refuge as a shelter from danger; a court as the retinue of a prince; recantation as the retracting of a declaration; constancy as fixedness in affection or purpose; and hospitality as the kind reception of guests.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger.
COURT, n. The persons who compose the retinue or council of a king or emperor; the hall or chamber where justice is administered.
RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a retraction of a declaration or proposition; the declaration that contradicts a former one.
CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; steadiness; immutability; firmness of mind, particularly in love or friendship.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, with kindness and liberality.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Rom 16:2
That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Este duchy where Renee of France sheltered evangelicals and corresponded with Calvin, and the seat of the 1438 council before its transfer to Florence.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern habit of reading a woman like Renee only as an ornament of her husband's court, or alternatively of making her a modern heroine detached from her confession. She was neither. She was a duchess who read, who kept a pastor, who asked Calvin hard questions and received hard answers, and who was broken once and did not stay broken. The sentence Hebrews pronounces over hunted believers covers a princess under house arrest as readily as a prophet in a cave: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:)” (Heb 11:38).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the office of the household in sheltering the church. Paul commends Phebe in terms of practical service and asks the church to receive her, “That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints” (Rom 16:2), and the general duty is stated without qualification: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2). What made Renee's hospitality more than kindness was the content she held to through it, which is Paul's charge to Timothy: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13). A refuge with no doctrine in it is only a comfortable house.

pos: n. (the Piedmontese capital of the house of Savoy, from which the dukes conducted the persecutions of the Waldensian valleys)
etymology: From Latin Augusta Taurinorum, the Augustan city of the Taurini, a Ligurian people.
biblical_def: Turin is the capital of Piedmont and from 1563 the seat of the dukes of Savoy, who moved their court there from Chambery. Its importance to this dictionary is that the orders which fell on the Waldensian valleys came from Turin. Emanuel Philibert's edict of 1560 required conformity and produced the campaign of 1560 and 1561 that ended in the peace of Cavour, the first legal recognition the Waldenses ever obtained. The pattern repeated: the edict of 1655 and the massacres called the Piedmontese Easter, which drew Cromwell's protest and Milton's sonnet; the expulsion of 1686 after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, when some three thousand survivors walked to Geneva over winter passes; and the Glorieuse Rentree of 1689, when about nine hundred of them came back and fought their way home. Civil rights were not granted until 1848. The dictionary records Turin because the long Waldensian endurance is the single clearest case in Europe of a confessing church outlasting a state determined to end it, and because the state in question was not heathen but Christian.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edict as a public ordinance of a sovereign; persecution as the infliction of pain for religion; endurance as continuance under suffering; a valley as a hollow between hills; and toleration as the allowance of what is not approved.
webster_full: EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order, command or ordinance by authority.
PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
ENDURANCE, n. Continuance; a bearing or suffering; a state of enduring pain or distress.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: Piedmontese capital of the house of Savoy, from which came the edicts and campaigns against the Waldensian valleys from 1560 to 1686.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is persecution conducted by a Christian state as an act of piety, and the dictionary names it as murder. The dukes of Savoy were not pagans; they acted on the advice of churchmen, with crusading language, against a people whose offence was reading the Scriptures in their own valleys. John sees that company in a particular place with a particular description: “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9). The altar locates them: their deaths were worship, not accident.

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The victory John describes is not survival but faithfulness through death, “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11), and the honour roll of Hebrews includes exactly the Waldensian experience of mountain exile: “they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented” (Heb 11:37). The ground on which a valley refuses a duke's edict is the apostolic answer to a council: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The dictionary adds that toleration in Piedmont came in 1848, which is late, and was a recognition of a church that had already won.

pos: n. (the Piedmontese city and commune, a station on the road from the Waldensian valleys to the Alpine passes and the Savoyard court)
etymology: From Latin Hasta Pompeia, a Roman town of Liguria, the name of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Asti is a Piedmontese city between Turin and Alessandria, a wealthy free commune in the thirteenth century with bankers active as far as Flanders, afterwards held by the Visconti, by France, and from 1531 by Savoy. It stood on the roads along which the Savoyard state administered and policed the Waldensian valleys, and its bishops and courts were part of the machinery by which the edicts out of Turin were enforced. Asti belongs in the dictionary as the ordinary case rather than the dramatic one: a respectable Italian city, neither a centre of evangelical reading nor a theatre of massacre, whose officials filled in the forms by which other men's houses were taken and other men's children baptised against their parents' conscience. The Reformation's witness is usually told through its martyrs and its reformers. The dictionary insists on also naming the mass of the baptised who did the paperwork, because that is the position most Christians in most generations actually occupy, and because Scripture addresses it directly and without flattery.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a magistrate as a public civil officer; an office as a particular duty or charge; complicity is not in Webster, but an accomplice is one associated in a crime; neutrality as a state of indifference; and duty as that which a person owes.
webster_full: MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
OFFICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose; a place of trust.
ACCOMPLICE, n. An associate in a crime; a partner or partaker in guilt.
NEUTRALITY, n. A state of indifference, or of neither friendship nor hostility; the condition of a nation which takes no part in a contest.
DUTY, n. That which a person owes to another; that which a person is bound by any natural, moral or legal obligation to pay, do or perform.
scriptures: Jas 4:17
Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.
If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
corruption_summary: Piedmontese city on the roads by which Turin's edicts against the Waldensian valleys were administered, and the dictionary's case study in ordinary complicity.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the belief that a man who does not strike a blow has no part in what his office accomplishes. The notaries, captains and curates of towns like Asti registered the confiscations, mustered the levies and received the forcibly baptised, and if asked would have said truly that they killed nobody. James removes that defence in one line: “Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin” (Jas 4:17). Solomon makes the omission specific and dreadful, charging his reader to “deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that there is no neutral ground in a persecution. Paul requires not only abstention but exposure, “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11), which is a far harder command than the one most officials obeyed. Joshua's demand on a divided assembly is the form the choice always takes: “choose you this day whom ye will serve” (Jos 24:15). He then answers it himself, household by household, “but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). The dictionary names Asti not to condemn a particular town but to refuse the comfort of the middle.
